blocks.text: A room, which has always been called the nursery. One of the doors leads into Anya’s room. Dawn, sun rises during the scene. May, the cherry trees in flower, but it is cold in the garden with the frost of early morning. Windows closed.
The train’s in, thank God. What time is it?
turns over the pages of the book
The dogs have been awake all night, they feel that the mistress is coming.
Why, what’s the matter with you, Dunyasha?
My hands are all of a tremble. I feel as though I should faint.
You’re a spoilt soft creature, Dunyasha. And dressed like a lady too, and your hair done up. That’s not the thing. One must know one’s place.
Oh, shut up! Don’t bother me.
Every day some misfortune befalls me. I don’t complain, I’m used to it, and I wear a smiling face.
stumbles against a chair, which falls over
Do you know, Yermolay Alexeyevitch, I must confess, Epihodov has made me a proposal.

I’m sure I don’t know.﻿ ﻿… He’s a harmless fellow, but sometimes when he begins talking, there’s no making anything of it. It’s all very fine and expressive, only there’s no understanding it. I’ve a sort of liking for him too. He loves me to distraction. He’s an unfortunate man; every day there’s something. They tease him about it﻿—two and twenty misfortunes they call him.
They really are coming. Let’s go and meet them. Will she know me? It’s five years since I saw her.
Let’s come in here. Do you remember what room this is, mamma?
The train was two hours late. What do you think of that? Is that the way to do things?
I haven’t slept for four nights on the journey. I feel dreadfully cold.
Epihodov, the clerk, made me a proposal just after Easter.
I don’t know what to think, really. He does love me, he does love me so!
Pyotr Sergeyevitch came the day before yesterday.
Dunyasha, coffee and make haste.﻿ ﻿… Mamma’s asking for coffee.
I have had a time of it!
We set off in Holy Week﻿—it was so cold then, and all the way Charlotta would talk and show off her tricks. What did you want to burden me with Charlotta for?
You couldn’t have travelled all alone, darling. At seventeen!

We got to Paris at last, it was cold there﻿—snow. I speak French shockingly. Mamma lives on the fifth floor, I went up to her, and there were a lot of French people, ladies, an old priest with a book. The place smelt of tobacco and so comfortless. I felt sorry, oh! so sorry for mamma all at once, I put my arms round her neck, and hugged her and wouldn’t let her go. Mamma was as kind as she could be, and she cried.﻿ ﻿…

She had sold her villa at Mentone, she had nothing left, nothing. I hadn’t a farthing left either, we only just had enough to get here. And mamma doesn’t understand! When we had dinner at the stations, she always ordered the most expensive things and gave the waiters a whole rouble. Charlotta’s just the same. Yasha too must have the same as we do; it’s simply awful. You know Yasha is mamma’s valet now, we brought him here with us.
Yes, I’ve seen the young rascal.
Well, tell me﻿—have you paid the arrears on the mortgage?
How could we get the money?
In August the place will be sold.
Peeps in at the door and moo’s like a cow.
Goes into her own room and in a lighthearted childish tone.
My darling’s home again! My pretty is home again!
The birds are singing in the garden. What time is it?
I shouldn’t have known you, Yasha. How you have changed abroad.
In the doorway, in a tone of vexation.
I told them not to wake him.
Goes up to the coffe-pot, anxiously.
How does it go? Let me remember. Cannon off the red!
That’s it﻿—in off the white! Why, once, sister, we used to sleep together in this very room, and now I’m fifty-one, strange as it seems.
Aye, it’s a long journey, to be sure.
draws her to her and kisses her
Covers her face with her hands.
I have to set off for Harkov directly, at five o’clock.﻿ ﻿… It is annoying! I wanted to have a look at you, and a little talk.﻿ ﻿… You are just as splendid as ever.

Your brother, Leonid Andreyevitch here, is always saying that I’m a lowborn knave, that I’m a moneygrubber, but I don’t care one straw for that. Let him talk. Only I do want you to believe in me as you used to. I do want your wonderful tender eyes to look at me as they used to in the old days. Merciful God! My father was a serf of your father and of your grandfather, but you﻿—you﻿—did so much for me once, that I’ve forgotten all that; I love you as though you were my kin﻿ ﻿… more than my kin.
jumps up and walks about in violent agitation
Nurse died while you were away.
takes a box of caramels out of his pocket and sucks one
My daughter, Dashenka, wishes to be remembered to you.
That’s all rot, if you’ll excuse me.
I don’t quite understand you, Yermolay Alexeyevitch.

You will get a rent of at least twenty-five roubles a year for a three-acre plot from summer visitors, and if you say the word now, I’ll bet you what you like there won’t be one square foot of ground vacant by the autumn, all the plots will be taken up. I congratulate you; in fact, you are saved. It’s a perfect situation with that deep river. Only, of course, it must be cleared﻿—all the old buildings, for example, must be removed, this house too, which is really good for nothing, and the old cherry orchard must be cut down.
Cut down? My dear fellow, forgive me, but you don’t know what you are talking about. If there is one thing interesting﻿—remarkable indeed﻿—in the whole province, it’s just our cherry orchard.
The only thing remarkable about the orchard is that it’s a very large one. There’s a crop of cherries every alternate year, and then there’s nothing to be done with them, no one buys them.
In old days, forty or fifty years ago, they used to dry the cherries, soak them, pickle them, make jam too, and they used﻿—

And they used to send the preserved cherries to Moscow and to Harkov by the wagon-load. That brought the money in! And the preserved cherries in those days were soft and juicy, sweet and fragrant.﻿ ﻿… They knew the way to do them then.﻿ ﻿…
And where is the recipe now?

There used to be only the gentlefolks and the peasants in the country, but now there are these summer visitors. All the towns, even the small ones, are surrounded nowadays by these summer villas. And one may say for sure, that in another twenty years there’ll be many more of these people and that they’ll be everywhere. At present the summer visitor only drinks tea in his verandah, but maybe he’ll take to working his bit of land too, and then your cherry orchard would become happy, rich and prosperous.﻿ ﻿…
takes out keys and opens an old-fashioned bookcase with a loud crack
tears the telegrams, without reading them
You are just the same as ever, Leonid.
takes the pillbox, pours the pills into the hollow of his hand, blows on them, puts them in his mouth and drinks off some kvass
I have taken all the pills.
He has taken to muttering like that for the last three years. We are used to it.
Charlotta, do show us some tricks!
Lowborn knave! I beg pardon, though﻿ ﻿… Varya is going to marry him, he’s Varya’s fiancé.
Well, Varya, I shall be delighted. He’s a good man.
snores, but at once wakes up
Well, we’ve finished our coffee, we can go to bed.
Looking out of the window into the garden.
H’m! and the orchard will be sold to pay our debts; it seems strange.﻿ ﻿…
There is no one. It was my fancy. On the right there, by the path to the arbour, there is a white tree bending like a woman.﻿ ﻿…
What a ravishing orchard! White masses of blossom, blue sky.﻿ ﻿…
Petya Trofimov, who was your Grisha’s tutor.﻿ ﻿… Can I have changed so much?
My Grisha﻿ ﻿… my boy﻿ ﻿… Grisha﻿ ﻿… my son!
We can’t help it, mamma, it is God’s will.
A peasant-woman in the train called me a mangy-looking gentleman.
I seem likely to be a perpetual student.
240 roubles﻿ ﻿… to pay the interest on my mortgage.
My dear man, I have no money.
I’ll pay it back, my dear﻿ ﻿… a trifling sum.
Oh, well, Leonid will give it you.﻿ ﻿… You give him the money, Leonid.
Me give it him! Let him wait till he gets it!
It can’t be helped, give it him. He needs it. He’ll pay it back.
Mamma’s just the same as ever, she hasn’t changed a bit. If she had her own way, she’d give away everything.
Don’t blubber. Aunt’s very rich, but she doesn’t like us. First, sister married a lawyer instead of a nobleman.﻿ ﻿…

And then her conduct, one can’t call it virtuous. She is good, and kind, and nice, and I love her, but, however one allows for extenuating circumstances, there’s no denying that she’s an immoral woman. One feels it in her slightest gesture.

I believe you, uncle. Everyone loves you and respects you﻿ ﻿… but, uncle dear, you must be silent﻿ ﻿… simply be silent. What were you saying just now about my mother, about your own sister? What made you say that?
puts his hand over his face
It’s true, uncle, you ought to keep quiet. Don’t talk, that’s all.
If you could keep from talking, it would make things easier for you, too.
If the Lord would help us!
puts a caramel in his mouth
Her equanimity has returned, she is quite happy.
Uncle dear, you’d better be quiet!
’Sh! She’s asleep, asleep. Come, my own.

The open country. An old shrine, long abandoned and fallen out of the perpendicular; near it a well, large stones that have apparently once been tombstones, and an old garden seat. The road to Gaev’s house is seen. On one side rise dark poplars; and there the cherry orchard begins. In the distance a row of telegraph poles and far, far away on the horizon there is faintly outlined a great town, only visible in very fine clear weather. It is near sunset. Charlotta, Yasha and Dunyasha are sitting on the seat. Epihodov is standing near, playing something mournful on a guitar. All sit plunged in thought. Charlotta wears an old forage cap; she has taken a gun from her shoulder and is tightening the buckle on the strap.
takes a cucumber out of her pocket and eats
Plays on the guitar and sings.
looks in a hand-mirror and powders herself
How shockingly these people sing! Foo! Like jackals!
That’s comprehensible. In foreign lands everything has long since reached full complexion.
takes guitar and goes off playing on it

You must make up your mind once for all﻿—there’s no time to lose. It’s quite a simple question, you know. Will you consent to letting the land for building or not? One word in answer: Yes or no? Only one word!

Pray do, Yasha. And what did I go off to the town to lunch for? Your restaurant’s a wretched place with its music and the tablecloth smelling of soap.﻿ ﻿… Why drink so much, Leonid? And eat so much? And talk so much? Today you talked a great deal again in the restaurant, and all so inappropriately. About the era of the ’seventies, about the decadents. And to whom? Talking to waiters about decadents!
hardly able to suppress his laughter
Deriganov, the millionaire, means to buy your estate. They say he is coming to the sale himself.
That’s what they say in town.
Our aunt in Yaroslavl has promised to send help; but when, and how much she will send, we don’t know.
How much will she send? A hundred thousand? Two hundred?
Oh, well!﻿ ﻿… Ten or fifteen thousand, and we must be thankful to get that.

Forgive me, but such reckless people as you are﻿—such queer, unbusiness-like people﻿—I never met in my life. One tells you in plain Russian your estate is going to be sold, and you seem not to understand it.
What are we to do? Tell us what to do.

I do tell you every day. Every day I say the same thing. You absolutely must let the cherry orchard and the land on building leases; and do it at once, as quick as may be﻿—the auction’s close upon us! Do understand! Once make up your mind to build villas, and you can raise as much money as you like, and then you are saved.
Villas and summer visitors﻿—forgive me saying so﻿—it’s so vulgar.
There I perfectly agree with you.
What is there to think of?
You have no sins to repent of.
Puts a caramel in his mouth.
Takes a telegram out of her pocket.
That’s our famous Jewish orchestra. You remember, four violins, a flute and a double bass.
That still in existence? We ought to send for them one evening, and give a dance.
And most likely there was nothing funny in it. You shouldn’t look at plays, you should look at yourselves a little oftener. How grey your lives are! How much nonsense you talk.
You ought to get married, my dear fellow.
You should marry our Varya, she’s a good girl.
She’s a good-natured girl, she’s busy all day long, and what’s more, she loves you. And you have liked her for ever so long.
I’ve been offered a place in the bank: 6,000 roubles a year. Did you know?
You would never do for that! You must stay as you are.
Put it on, sir, it’s damp.
Those were fine old times. There was flogging anyway.
Hold your tongue, Firs. I must go to town tomorrow. I have been promised an introduction to a general, who might let us have a loan.
You won’t bring that off. And you won’t pay your arrears, you may rest assured of that.
That’s all his nonsense. There is no such general.
Our perpetual student is always with the young ladies.
He’ll soon be fifty, and he’s still a student.
Why are you so cross, you queer fish?

I’ll tell you my idea of you, Yermolay Alexeyevitch: you are a rich man, you’ll soon be a millionaire. Well, just as in the economy of nature a wild beast is of use, who devours everything that comes in his way, so you too have your use.
Better tell us something about the planets, Petya.
No, let us go on with the conversation we had yesterday.

We had a long conversation yesterday, but we came to no conclusion. In pride, in your sense of it, there is something mystical. Perhaps you are right from your point of view; but if one looks at it simply, without subtlety, what sort of pride can there be, what sense is there in it, if man in his physiological formation is very imperfect, if in the immense majority of cases he is coarse, dull-witted, profoundly unhappy? One must give up glorification of self. One should work, and nothing else.
One must die in any case.
Who knows? And what does it mean﻿—dying? Perhaps man has a hundred senses, and only the five we know are lost at death, while the other ninety-five remain alive.

Humanity progresses, perfecting its powers. Everything that is beyond its ken now will one day become familiar and comprehensible; only we must work, we must with all our powers aid the seeker after truth. Here among us in Russia the workers are few in number as yet. The vast majority of the intellectual people I know, seek nothing, do nothing, are not fit as yet for work of any kind. They call themselves intellectual, but they treat their servants as inferiors, behave to the peasants as though they were animals, learn little, read nothing seriously, do practically nothing, only talk about science and know very little about art. They are all serious people, they all have severe faces, they all talk of weighty matters and air their theories, and yet the vast majority of us﻿—ninety-nine percent﻿—live like savages, at the least thing fly to blows and abuse, eat piggishly, sleep in filth and stuffiness, bugs everywhere, stench and damp and moral impurity. And it’s clear all our fine talk is only to divert our attention and other people’s. Show me where to find the crèches there’s so much talk about, and the reading-rooms? They only exist in novels: in real life there are none of them. There is nothing but filth and vulgarity and Asiatic apathy. I fear and dislike very serious faces. I’m afraid of serious conversations. We should do better to be silent.

You know, I get up at five o’clock in the morning, and I work from morning to night; and I’ve money, my own and other people’s, always passing through my hands, and I see what people are made of all round me. One has only to begin to do anything to see how few honest, decent people there are. Sometimes when I lie awake at night, I think: “Oh! Lord, thou hast given us immense forests, boundless plains, the widest horizons, and living here we ourselves ought really to be giants.”
You ask for giants! They are no good except in storybooks; in real life they frighten us.
The sun has set, my friends.
Not loudly, but, as it were, declaiming.
Uncle, you are at it again!
You’d much better be cannoning off the red!
I’ll hold my tongue, I will.
I don’t know. Somewhere far away a bucket fallen and broken in the pits. But somewhere very far away.
It might be a bird of some sort﻿—such as a heron.
It was the same before the calamity﻿—the owl hooted and the samovar hissed all the time.
Allow me to inquire, can I get to the station this way?
There’s no doing anything with me. I’m so silly! When we get home, I’ll give you all I possess. Yermolay Alexeyevitch, you will lend me some more﻿ ﻿… !
Come, friends, it’s time to be going. And Varya, we have made a match of it for you. I congratulate you.
My hands are trembling; it’s a long while since I had a game of billiards.
“Ophelia! Nymph, in thy orisons be all my sins remember’d.”
Come, it will soon be suppertime.
How he frightened me! My heart’s simply throbbing.
Let me remind you, ladies and gentlemen: on the 22nd of August the cherry orchard will be sold. Think about that! Think about it!

Varya’s afraid we shall fall in love with each other, and for days together she won’t leave us. With her narrow brain she can’t grasp that we are above love. To eliminate the petty and transitory which hinders us from being free and happy﻿—that is the aim and meaning of our life. Forward! We go forward irresistibly towards the bright star that shines yonder in the distance. Forward! Do not lag behind, friends.
Somehow, Petya, you’ve made me so that I don’t love the cherry orchard as I used to. I used to love it so dearly. I used to think that there was no spot on earth like our garden.
The house we live in has long ceased to be our own, and I shall leave it, I give you my word.
If you have the house keys, fling them into the well and go away. Be free as the wind.

Believe me, Anya, believe me! I am not thirty yet, I am young, I am still a student, but I have gone through so much already! As soon as winter comes I am hungry, sick, careworn, poor as a beggar, and what ups and downs of fortune have I not known! And my soul was always, every minute, day and night, full of inexplicable forebodings. I have a foreboding of happiness, Anya. I see glimpses of it already.
Well, let’s go down to the river. It’s lovely there.

A drawing-room divided by an arch from a larger drawing-room. A chandelier burning. The Jewish orchestra, the same that was mentioned in Act II, is heard playing in the anteroom. It is evening. In the larger drawing-room they are dancing the grand chain. The voice of Seyonov-Pishtchik: “Promenade à une paire!” Then enter the drawing-room in couples, first Pishtchik and Charlotta Ivanovna, then Trofimov and Lyubov Andreyevna, thirdly Anya with the Post-Office Clerk, fourthly Varya with the Station Master, and other guests. Varya is quietly weeping and wiping away her tears as she dances. In the last couple is Dunyasha. They move across the drawing-room. Pishtchik shouts: “Grand rond, balancez!” and “Les Cavaliers à genou et remerciez vos dames.”
snores, but at once wakes up
There really is something horsy about your appearance.
Well﻿ ﻿… a horse is a fine beast﻿ ﻿… a horse can be sold.
Yes, I am a mangy-looking gentleman, and I’m proud of it!
Nietzsche, the philosopher, a very great and celebrated man﻿ ﻿… of enormous intellect﻿ ﻿… says in his works, that one can make forged banknotes.
feels in his pockets, in alarm
The sale hasn’t taken place, most likely.
Taking a card out of his breast pocket.
Claps her hands, pack of cards disappears.
A mysterious feminine voice which seems coming out of the floor answers her. “Oh, yes, it’s magnificent weather, madam.”
And I greatly admire you too, madam.
Takes a travelling rug from a chair.

And still Leonid doesn’t come. I can’t understand what he’s doing in the town so long! Why, everything must be over by now. The estate is sold, or the sale has not taken place. Why keep us so long in suspense?
Great-aunt sent him an authorisation to buy it in her name, and transfer the debt. She’s doing it for Anya’s sake, and I’m sure God will be merciful. Uncle will buy it.
hides her face in her hands
Why are you angry, Varya? He’s teasing you about Lopahin. Well, what of that? Marry Lopahin if you like, he’s a good man, and interesting; if you don’t want to, don’t! Nobody compels you, darling.
I must tell you plainly, mamma, I look at the matter seriously; he’s a good man, I like him.
Well, marry him. I can’t see what you’re waiting for.

Mamma, I can’t make him an offer myself. For the last two years, everyone’s been talking to me about him. Everyone talks; but he says nothing or else makes a joke. I see what it means. He’s growing rich, he’s absorbed in business, he has no thoughts for me. If I had money, were it ever so little, if I had only a hundred roubles, I’d throw everything up and go far away. I would go into a nunnery.
In a soft tone with tears.
Don’t tease her, Petya. You see she has grief enough without that.

She is so very officious, meddling in what’s not her business. All the summer she’s given Anya and me no peace. She’s afraid of a love affair between us. What’s it to do with her? Besides, I have given no grounds for it. Such triviality is not in my line. We are above love!

What does it matter whether the estate is sold today or not? That’s all done with long ago. There’s no turning back, the path is overgrown. Don’t worry yourself, dear Lyubov Andreyevna. You mustn’t deceive yourself; for once in your life you must face the truth!
You know I feel for you with all my heart.
takes out her handkerchief, telegram falls on the floor
He is a wretch! You’re the only person that doesn’t know it! He’s a worthless creature! A despicable wretch!
Getting angry, but speaking with restraint.
I am above love! You’re not above love, but simply as our Firs here says, “You are a good-for-nothing.” At your age not to have a mistress!
Goes rapidly into the larger drawing-room clutching his head.
Goes off, but at once returns.
What a queer fellow that Petya is!

I don’t feel well. In old days we used to have generals, barons and admirals dancing at our balls, and now we send for the post-office clerk and the station master and even they’re not overanxious to come. I am getting feeble. The old master, the grandfather, used to give sealing-wax for all complaints. I have been taking sealing-wax for twenty years or more. Perhaps that’s what’s kept me alive.
He didn’t say to whom. He’s gone away.
There was an old man gossiping there, a stranger.
I feel as though I should die. Go, Yasha, find out to whom it has been sold.
Epihodov is so funny. He’s a silly fellow, two and twenty misfortunes.
Firs, if the estate is sold, where will you go?
Where you bid me, there I’ll go.
Why do you look like that? Are you ill? You ought to be in bed.
looking about him; in an undertone
They pass into the larger room.
In the larger drawing-room, a figure in a grey top hat and in check trousers is gesticulating and jumping about. Shouts of “Bravo, Charlotta Ivanovna.”
She has stopped to powder herself.
What did he say to you?
He said I was like a flower.
Like a flower. I am a girl of such delicate feelings, I am awfully fond of soft speeches.
I have a misfortune every day, and if I may venture to express myself, I merely smile at it, I even laugh.
You really cannot, if I may so express myself, call me to account like this.
I’m not calling you to account, I’m speaking to you. You do nothing but wander from place to place and don’t do your work. We keep you as a countinghouse clerk, but what use you are I can’t say.
He goes towards the door, she following him.
Not at all! I humbly thank you for your kind reception!
moves away, then looks round and asks softly
Oh, no! Not at all! There’s an immense bump coming up, though!
Is it you, Yermolay Alexeyevitch? Why have you been so long? Where’s Leonid?
Leonid Andreyevitch arrived with me. He is coming.
Embarrassed, afraid of betraying his joy.
goes to his own room across the larger drawing-room
How about the sale? Tell us, do!
The orchestra is heard tuning up.
Takes him by the arm, in an undertone.
takes him by the arm and leads him into the larger drawing-room
Accidentally tips over a little table, almost upsetting the candelabra.

Mamma! Mamma, you’re crying, dear, kind, good mamma! My precious! I love you! I bless you! The cherry orchard is sold, it is gone, that’s true, that’s true! But don’t weep, mamma! Life is still before you, you have still your good, pure heart! Let us go, let us go, darling, away from here! We will make a new garden, more splendid than this one; you will see it, you will understand. And joy, quiet, deep joy, will sink into your soul like the sun at evening! And you will smile, mamma! Come, darling, let us go!

Scene: Same as in First Act. There are neither curtains on the windows nor pictures on the walls: only a little furniture remains piled up in a corner as if for sale. There is a sense of desolation; near the outer door and in the background of the scene are packed trunks, travelling bags, etc. On the left the door is open, and from here the voices of Varya and Anya are audible. Lopahin is standing waiting. Yasha is holding a tray with glasses full of champagne. In front of the stage Epihodov is tying up a box. In the background behind the scene a hum of talk from the peasants who have come to say goodbye. The voice of Gaev: “Thanks, brothers, thanks!”
The peasants have come to say goodbye. In my opinion, Yermolay Alexeyevitch, the peasants are good-natured, but they don’t know much about things.
You gave them your purse, Lyuba. That won’t do﻿—that won’t do!
I couldn’t help it! I couldn’t help it!
In the doorway, calls after them.
Looks at his watch; says in doorway.

And I’m getting off to Harkov. I am going in the same train with you. I’m spending all the winter at Harkov. I’ve been wasting all my time gossiping with you and fretting with no work to do. I can’t get on without work. I don’t know what to do with my hands, they flap about so queerly, as if they didn’t belong to me.
Well, we’re just going away, and you will take up your profitable labours again.
Then you’re going to Moscow now?
Yes. I shall see them as far as the town, and tomorrow I shall go on to Moscow.
Yes, I daresay, the professors aren’t giving any lectures, they’re waiting for your arrival.
How many years have you been at the University?
What for? I don’t need it.
Why, you haven’t got a halfpenny.
Flings a pair of goloshes on to the stage.
Why are you so cross, Varya? h’m!﻿ ﻿… but those aren’t my goloshes.

I sowed three thousand acres with poppies in the spring, and now I have cleared forty thousand profit. And when my poppies were in flower, wasn’t it a picture! So here, as I say, I made forty thousand, and I’m offering you a loan because I can afford to. Why turn up your nose? I am a peasant﻿—I speak bluntly.
In the distance is heard the stroke of an axe on a tree.

Goodbye, my dear fellow; it’s time to be off. We turn up our noses at one another, but life is passing all the while. When I am working hard without resting, then my mind is more at ease, and it seems to me as though I too know what I exist for; but how many people there are in Russia, my dear boy, who exist, one doesn’t know what for. Well, it doesn’t matter. That’s not what keeps things spinning. They tell me Leonid Andreyevitch has taken a situation. He is going to be a clerk at the bank﻿—6,000 roubles a year. Only, of course, he won’t stick to it﻿—he’s too lazy.
walks out across the front of the stage
Has Firs been taken to the hospital?
I told them this morning. No doubt they have taken him.
puts a trunk down on a cardboard hatbox and crushes it
Why wasn’t the note for the doctor taken too?
weeps and throws herself on his neck
Powders her face, looking in a pocket-mirror.
casts a look about the room
Very glad! A new life is beginning, mamma.

Yes, really, everything is all right now. Before the cherry orchard was sold, we were all worried and wretched, but afterwards, when once the question was settled conclusively, irrevocably, we all felt calm and even cheerful.
